note:
A fresh check found these problems in this version. Fix each one, and keep everything that is right:
- Question b, wording: The distractor 'As a place locals must leave to find a café or motel' uses 'must', and the card speaks in terms of 'can' and 'may'. The absolute word helps mark this option as wrong without any need to know the idea.
- Question b, other: Wilga is a real locality in Western Australia (Shire of Boyup Brook), but the question presents a made-up new highway and new businesses there as if they happened. A fictional town name, or a clear 'imagine' framing, would avoid teaching students something false about a real place.

rejected.title: Transport and access
card: Access is how easily people can reach jobs, services and other places. Roads, flights and public transport all shape it.
Good transport shortens the time and cost of a trip. A place with frequent trains or buses is easier to reach than one with no regular service.
Poor access can leave people far from hospitals, schools and work. Some remote towns depend on a long road or a small plane to reach them.
Transport also changes how people use and see a place. A new road can bring visitors and new businesses, so a quiet town may come to be seen as a busy stop.
rejected.remember: Better transport means easier access, and that changes how a place is used and seen.

a.q: Two towns are the same distance from a city hospital. One has a train every hour. The other has no regular service. Which is true?
opts: The town with the train has better access
Both towns have the same access to the hospital
The town without the train has better access
Neither town has any access to the hospital
a.why: Access is about how easily people can reach a place, not just how far away it is. Frequent trains cut the time and cost of the trip, so that town has better access. Equal distance does not mean equal access.
a.clue: Access depends on more than distance.

b.q: A new highway is built past Wilga, a quiet farming town in Western Australia. Cafés and motels open for drivers. How might people now see Wilga?
opts: As a stopover town for people on the highway
As a remote town that is hard to reach by road
As a farming town no one outside the area visits
As a place locals must leave to find a café or motel
b.why: The highway made Wilga easier to reach, and the new cafés and motels serve drivers who stop there. So the town is used and seen as a stopover. It was once a quiet farming town, but the new businesses show outsiders now visit.
b.clue: Who are the new businesses there to serve?

a.q: Why does a remote town with no regular bus or train service often have poor access?
opts: Residents take longer and pay more to reach services
Residents are barred from using hospitals in other towns
Residents choose to avoid jobs and schools elsewhere
Residents cannot see the town's surrounding landscape
a.why: Without regular transport, trips to jobs and services take more time and cost more. The town is not cut off by rules or by choice, so the options about being barred or choosing to avoid are wrong.
a.clue: Think about the time and cost of each trip.

b.q: A new highway is built past Wilga, a quiet farming town in Western Australia. Cafés and motels open for travellers. What has the highway most directly changed?
opts: How the town is used and seen, as a stop for travellers
How far the town sits from the nearest coast
How much rain falls on the surrounding farmland
How many people use the town's old airstrip
b.why: The highway improved access, which brought travellers and new businesses, so the town is used and seen differently. The highway cannot move the town or change the rainfall, and nothing in the case says airstrip use changed.
b.clue: Which change comes from people being able to reach the town?

a.best: Residents take longer and pay more to reach services

b.best: How the town is used and seen, as a stop for travellers

problems.detail: The right option is clearly the longest and the only one with an extra detail ('as a stop for travellers'). It also echoes 'travellers' from the stem and 'used and seen' from the card, so a student could pick it without knowing the idea.
The distractors (distance to the coast, rainfall) are things a highway obviously cannot change, which makes the question too easy for Year 9.
The clue 'Think about the time and cost of each trip' points straight to the only option that mentions time and cost, which gives the answer away.
